title: VCF Automation 9.1 catalog provisioning that survives being re-run
prompt:
Our platform team provisions from the VCF Automation 9.1 catalog (the VCF 9.1 successor to vRealize and Aria Automation) out of jobs that get re-run — by hand, by cron, and by whatever restarted them after a network blip. Write the PowerShell module those jobs call.

The repository already has what you need:

- `docs/contract.json` is the wire contract for the three API operations you may use. Treat it as authoritative for methods, paths, parameter names, property names, types and authentication. Note where it came from: VCF Automation publishes no OpenAPI specification, so the contract was transcribed by hand from the reference pages recorded in `docs/official_sources.json`. Read both — the contract flags the one place the reference contradicts itself.
- `mock/` is a loopback stand-in for an appliance. It is pinned to the contract, serves nothing the contract does not name, and records every request it receives.
- `tests/verify.py` is the acceptance test. Run it with `python3 tests/verify.py`; it starts the stand-in for you on an ephemeral loopback port. Run `bash scripts/setup.sh` first to install the PowerCLI prerequisite.

Read `README.md` for the layout.

## What to build

A PowerShell module at `src/VcfAutomationCatalog/`, with the manifest `VcfAutomationCatalog.psd1`, exporting exactly one function:

```
New-VcfAutomationCatalogDeployment
    -ApiUri              <string>       appliance root URL, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:8721
    -RefreshToken        <string>       API token issued from the VCF Automation UI
    -CatalogItemId       <string>
    -DeploymentName      <string>
    -ProjectId           <string>
    [-Inputs             <hashtable>]   blueprint inputs, however deeply nested
    [-Reason             <string>]
    [-CatalogItemVersion <string>]
```

Operation paths from the contract are appended to `-ApiUri` unchanged.

It returns exactly one object with:

- `DeploymentId` — id of the deployment the run ended up with
- `DeploymentName`
- `Created` — `$true` when this run's catalog request is what brought the deployment into existence, `$false` when it was already there before the run started
- `LookupCount` — how many times the run looked the deployment up

## Session

1. Exchange `-RefreshToken` for an access token once per run, using the contract's token operation. That call is what mints the token, so it carries no `Authorization` header of its own.
2. Authenticate every other call with the bearer scheme the contract describes, built from both fields the token response returns.

## The problem

The catalog request operation allocates a **new** deployment every time the appliance accepts it. The contract records that there is no idempotency key, no precondition header and no de-duplication window — nothing on the wire makes a resend safe. But these jobs do get re-run, and a duplicate deployment costs real capacity and takes an approval to unwind.

The deployment name is unique within a project, so that pair is the natural key. Build the retry safety out of it.

3. Before submitting anything, look the deployment up by name within the project. Send exactly two query parameters — the exact-name filter and the project filter — and nothing else.
4. If it is already there, return it and submit no catalog request at all. `Created` is `$false`.
5. Otherwise submit the catalog request, once.
6. **If that request fails in a way that leaves its outcome unknown — a 5xx, or an error that came back with no response at all — the deployment may exist anyway.** Do not resend it blind. Look it up again. If it has appeared, that is your request having landed after the answer was lost: adopt it and return it, with `Created` `$true`. Only resend when that second lookup still finds nothing, and resend at most once, byte for byte the same. If the resend fails too, throw.
7. A failure the appliance answered with a 4xx is it telling you it did nothing. That is a different situation; do not retry it.

## Mapping the arguments onto the request body

| Body field | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `deploymentName` | `-DeploymentName` |
| `projectId` | `-ProjectId` |
| `inputs` | `-Inputs` when it has entries, sent through unchanged however deeply it nests |
| `reason` | `-Reason` when it has a value |
| `version` | `-CatalogItemVersion` when it has a value |
| `bulkRequestCount` | never sent; this function requests one deployment |

## The omission rule

> Any optional field with no value must be left out of the JSON body entirely. Never send it as `null`, `""`, `[]` or `{}`.

The appliance reads a property that is *present* as an instruction, and the contract records that the reference documents no null semantics for this body.

## Packaging

The module manifest declares `VMware.Sdk.Vcf.SddcManager` in `RequiredModules`. The environment installs the `VMware.Sdk.Vcf` PowerCLI modules from the PowerShell Gallery via `scripts/setup.sh` — do not vendor, bundle or commit any copy of them. The auto-generated VCF PowerCLI SDK covers SDDC Manager, Operations, Installer and Cloud Builder but has no binding for VCF Automation, which is why the requests in this module are built by hand against `docs/contract.json`.

## Ground rules

Everything runs against `127.0.0.1`; no live VMware endpoint is involved. Add only `src/`; leave `docs/`, `mock/`, `tests/`, `scripts/` and `README.md` as they are.
